title: Monoclonal Magic & Plant Powers
welcome_lead: Stretch yourself today — monoclonal antibodies, plant defences, and where our best drugs come from.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Infection & Response stretch — monoclonal antibodies, plant defences, drug discovery.

concepts.def: Identical antibodies from one type of B cell
B cell fused with tumour cell — divides forever
Pregnancy hormone detected in urine tests
Waxy plant layer that blocks pathogens
Heart drug originally from foxglove plants

walkthroughs.body_html:
Monoclonal means one clone — identical antibodies, all targeting the same antigen.

How they're made: inject a mouse with the antigen → its B lymphocytes make antibodies → fuse one B cell with a fast-dividing tumour cell to form a hybridoma → the hybridoma divides forever, churning out identical antibodies.

Uses: pregnancy tests (detect hCG in urine), cancer treatment (carry drugs to tumour cells only), diagnosis (spot specific molecules in blood).

Plants can't run, so they defend themselves three ways.

Physical: a waxy cuticle, tough cellulose cell walls, and layers of bark.

Chemical: antibacterial chemicals (like mint oils) and poisons (like nicotine in tobacco).

Mechanical: thorns, hairs, and drooping or curling leaves when touched (e.g. Mimosa pudica).

Many modern drugs were first discovered in plants and microbes.

Digitalis — heart drug from the foxglove plant.

Aspirin — painkiller from willow bark.

Penicillin — discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from Penicillium mould on a Petri dish.

Today new drugs go through three test phases: preclinical (cells & animals), then clinical trials on healthy volunteers, then on patients. Double-blind trials use a placebo to remove bias.
